title: Catheter Management of Patent Foramen Ovale -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Patent foramen ovale (PFO) is a common abnormality that describes the presence of a small opening between the top two chambers of the heart. Several large, population-based studies estimate that transcatheter closure of PFO, in addition to medical therapy, is superior to medical therapy alone in preventing recurrent cryptogenic stroke. It is worth noting that PFO closure in these patients has not demonstrated a reduction in the risk of recurrent transient ischemic events (TIA) or all-cause mortality. This activity reviews the role of percutaneous closure of the PFO and its indications and contraindications. It highlights the role of the interprofessional team in managing patients with congenital heart defects.

title: Catheter Management of Patent Foramen Ovale -- Introduction
content: Patent foramen ovale (PFO) is a small opening between the top 2 chambers of the heart (see Image. Patent Foramen Ovale). However, it is one of the most common cardiac defects. Several large, population-based studies estimated no differences in incidence (at about 9.2%) between patients with stroke and patients without a stroke. [1] Patent foramen ovale is present in one-fifth of the population. They affect males and females equally. The size grows with age, whereas the prevalence diminishes with increasing age. [2] PFO has correlations with both cardiac and extra-cardiac disorders. Its strongest association seen in the literature is with cryptogenic stroke. The PFO provides a conduit for emboli to shunt from right to left. [3] Most present incidentally on echocardiogram following stroke workup. The contribution of the PFO to the burden of cryptogenic stroke is well-characterized. Several large, population-based studies estimate that transcatheter closure of PFO in addition to medical therapy is superior to medical therapy alone in preventing recurrent cryptogenic stroke; it bears mention that PFO closure in these patients has not demonstrated a reduction in the risk of recurrent TIA or all-cause mortality. Studies have found a higher rate of postoperative atrial fibrillation following PFO closure device placement, the long-term effects of which have yet to be studied. [4]

title: Catheter Management of Patent Foramen Ovale -- Introduction
content: Data exists showing that PFO closure for cryptogenic stroke can be cost-effective. [5] One study demonstrated that the effectiveness of PFO closure depends on the device used. [6] The gold standard for diagnosis of PFO remains a transoesophageal echocardiogram with a bubble test after a sustained Valsalva maneuver (see Video. Transesophageal Echocardiogram). Once identified, the structure can undergo an assessment to determine the need for treatment. There are surgical, transcatheter, and medical therapies available for treatment. The percutaneous transcatheter approach is becoming more favored, as most patients prefer the less invasive procedure.

title: Catheter Management of Patent Foramen Ovale -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: A patent foramen ovale is a remnant opening of the fetal foramen ovale. The foramen ovale is a conduit for blood to flow from the right atrium to the left atrium in the fetal state. Usually, the PFO closes at birth, but in about 25% percent of the population, it does not close. Within this subset, a few people experience symptoms or sequelae related to PFO patency. These patients should receive an evaluation for possible PFO closure.

title: Catheter Management of Patent Foramen Ovale -- Indications
content: Indications for transcatheter PFO closure: Recurrent cryptogenic stroke because of presumed paradoxical embolism Recurrent transient ischemic attacks (TIA) History of paradoxical peripheral embolism Decompression sickness Migraine [7]

title: Catheter Management of Patent Foramen Ovale -- Contraindications
content: Contraindications of percutaneous transcatheter PFO closure include, but are not limited to, the following: >25 mm PFO (refer for surgery) Active endocarditis Active bacteremia Active fungemia Current sepsis Intracardiac mass Intracardiac anatomy precluding safe device delivery [6]

title: Catheter Management of Patent Foramen Ovale -- Preparation
content: Preparation for percutaneous transcatheter PFO closure begins with an evaluation of the patient to determine if they qualify for catheter closure. This evaluation typically starts with cranial imaging, followed by an echocardiogram with a bubble study.  Additional pre-operative tests may include a chest x-ray, electrocardiogram, and blood tests to assess the patient's general health and kidney function. Before the procedure, all patients undergoing PFO closure should be pre-treated with antiplatelet therapy, commonly with both aspirin and Plavix daily. Warfarin therapy alone may be an option in patients who need chronic antithrombotic therapy followed by bridging with low-molecular-weight heparin before and after PFO closure. One hour before percutaneous access, an intravenous antibiotic dose should be administered, typically cefazolin or vancomycin, if the patient is allergic to penicillin. To avoid left atrial hypovolemia, patients should also receive IV normal saline before and during the procedure.

title: Catheter Management of Patent Foramen Ovale -- Technique or Treatment
content: The first step in the transcatheter PFO closure procedure is gaining access. The femoral venous site is the easiest, safest, and therefore the most commonly used site for performing PFO closure. It allows insertion of the occluder vertically from the inferior right atrium to the superior left atrium. After femoral venous sheath insertion, a heparin bolus is given to achieve anticoagulant properties. More heparin is used intermittently throughout the procedure to maintain anticoagulant activity. Oxygenation is administered via nasal cannula oxygen to achieve hyperoxygenation. Hyperoxygenation is preemptively treated in case of a possible air embolus during LA catheterization. A balloon-tipped angiographic catheter or pigtail catheter is inserted, and cineangiography is done to outline the left atrial (LA) anatomy. A 6-F multipurpose catheter is then advanced over a guide-wire into the superior vena cava (SVC). The catheter is then positioned posteriorly and withdrawn to the fossa ovalis.

title: Catheter Management of Patent Foramen Ovale -- Technique or Treatment
content: When the catheter is in the fossa ovalis, the guide wire advances across the PFO into the left superior pulmonary vein. The multipurpose catheter then gets advanced into this pulmonary vein, and its position is confirmed by hemodynamic measurement of LA pressure. In some circumstances, the guide wire is difficult to pass into the LA. In these circumstances, a different guide-wire might be used. The multipurpose catheter is then exchanged over a straight tetrafluoroethylene-coated stainless steel guide wire for the guide or a flex sheath placed in the left atrium. A sheathless approach is employed by removing both the multipurpose catheter and the femoral venous sheath. Many operators attach an accessory adapter to the guiding catheter to administer continuous saline hand flushing while advancing the guide to the left atrium. Tunnel length can be determined with gentle balloon sizing of the PFO.  After selecting the appropriate device, the LA disc is placed in the LA. The sheath and device are then drawn back until the LA disc attaches to the LA septum. With slight tension against the LA septum, the RA side of the device is then deployed. Contrast is pushed through the sheath beside the RA disc to confirm proper device positioning. The left anterior oblique projection is then used to view the discs. The space between the two discs is associated with the width of the septum secundum. After device release, RA angiography may be performed to assess the correct positioning and function of the implanted device.

title: Catheter Management of Patent Foramen Ovale -- Technique or Treatment
content: The data is inconclusive as to whether intracardiac or transesophageal echocardiographic guidance is better for PFO closure as compared to fluoroscopic guidance alone. One study confirms the efficacy and safety of TTE guidance during the percutaneous closure of PFO, which shortens procedural time and eliminates the need for general anesthesia or endotracheal intubation. [7] However, fluoroscopy guidance has been shown to increase the procedural time and cost associated with balloon sizing compared to TTE, which decreases both of these.

title: Catheter Management of Patent Foramen Ovale -- Technique or Treatment
content: After completion of the procedure, transthoracic echocardiography with a bubble study is used to confirm the device's positioning and assess for residual shunting. An electrocardiogram and chest X-ray are also useful for evaluating complications and the accuracy of the procedure. Anticoagulation therapy is given for 6 months post-operation. Dental procedures should be postponed for 6 months. If dental procedures are required, antibiotic prophylaxis should be given to prevent endocarditis within the first 6 months. Follow-up with transthoracic echocardiography is at 1 and 6 months following the procedure.

title: Catheter Management of Patent Foramen Ovale -- Complications
content: Data show that trans-catheter PFO closure complication rates are approximately 7%. Studies have shown that the incidence of an adverse event is higher in patients >60 years of age. Furthermore, adverse outcomes are higher in patients with a preceding ischemic stroke versus a transient ischemic stroke.  Complications include the following in order of most common to least: Arrhythmia (most commonly atrial fibrillation) Vascular complications Hemorrhage/hematoma Cardiac tamponade/perforation Loss of life Pneumothorax/hemothorax Occluder embolus Infection

title: Catheter Management of Patent Foramen Ovale -- Clinical Significance
content: Patent foramen ovale closure is not necessary for all patients. However, a select number of patients benefit significantly from PFO closure. The sequelae in this population are many times more devastating, especially in those with debilitating strokes. Therefore, primary care providers must recognize the indications for PFO closure and refer patients appropriately. Knowing that PFOs greater than 25 mm are usually not amenable to percutaneous management and more often require surgical closure is critical information to share with the patient. [6] In addition to indications and contraindications for PFO closure, every practitioner should be aware of the common post-op complications; arrhythmia is the most common, but death is also a possibility.

title: Catheter Management of Patent Foramen Ovale -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Percutaneous transcatheter closure of PFO, for the most part, is a safe and straightforward procedure. However, complications do occur. Therefore, it is essential to adopt an interprofessional approach to evaluation and determine which, if any, closure procedure the patients should undergo. For patient safety, it is critical to follow guideline recommendations when selecting a procedure or therapy. For best results, an interprofessional team should evaluate and treat the patient. A cardiology specialty nurse should assist with patient education and monitoring before, during, and after the procedure. A cardiology-trained pharmacist should assist with evaluating the patient for potential drug-drug interactions that may complicate the procedure. The team should include a specialty-trained cardiologist as well as a cardiothoracic surgeon to assist with complications. Utilizing an interprofessional team will yield the best results.
